My land is about 10 mu, flat ground on the North China Plain. My father grew wheat and corn here, and his father before him. The soil knows these two crops, and so do I.

I will do the winter wheat–summer maize rotation, same as every year, same as my neighbors. It makes sense: wheat goes in October, comes out in June. Then I plant maize straight into the stubble, harvest it in September, and start over. The land never sits idle. The county agricultural office pushes this rotation too, so I know it's the right call.

For wheat I'll use a Jimai improved variety — the seeds I got from the co-op last autumn are already sitting in my storage. For maize I'll use Zhengdan 958 hybrid seed, same as the past three years. It's reliable and the grain drying station accepts it without complaint.

Fertilizer: I put down compound fertilizer as basal, then top-dress urea at jointing for wheat and at small-horn stage for maize. I probably apply a bit more than I strictly need — I can't afford a bad harvest, and extra fertilizer feels like insurance.

Irrigation: wheat needs water before winter freeze, again at jointing, at heading, and at grain fill — four times. Maize usually gets one watering if summer rains fall short. I pump from the village well like everyone else.

I'll spray pesticide twice on wheat — once for aphids and powdery mildew in spring, once near heading if I see rust. Maize usually just needs one spray for corn borer.

Tillage: I rotary-till before wheat planting to break up the soil after maize harvest. For maize I go no-till — seeding straight in after wheat combines pass through saves me time and diesel.
